## Git as the single source of truth changes how you think about mistakes

Once cluster state is reconciled from a Git repository rather than applied by hand, a bad change becomes a revert instead of a scramble. That shift alone is worth the upfront setup cost — the safety net changes how confidently you're willing to experiment.

## Secrets are the hard part, not the manifests

Writing Kubernetes YAML is the easy 80%. Deciding how secrets get into a GitOps-reconciled cluster without ending up in Git history is the harder 20% — worth solving properly, with a real secrets backend, before the homelab has anything worth protecting.

## Reconciliation drift will happen — plan for detecting it, not preventing it

A manual `kubectl edit` during a late-night fix is inevitable. The goal isn't to prevent every manual change, it's to make sure the GitOps controller reliably reports and reverts drift so a manual fix doesn't silently become permanent, undocumented configuration.

## Small, incremental migrations beat a big-bang cutover

Migrating a homelab to GitOps one application at a time — proving the pattern on something low-stakes first — surfaces problems (ingress quirks, storage class mismatches, ordering dependencies) while the blast radius of a mistake is still small.

## The real value is the audit trail, not the automation

The most useful part of running a homelab this way isn't that changes apply automatically — it's that every change to the running state has a commit, an author, and a timestamp. That habit of "every change is a diff" is the part worth carrying into any environment, homelab or not.
